newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US presses Zaire rebels on access to refugees.
newsitem.headline: US presses Zaire rebels on access to refugees.

text.p: Washington has stepped up pressure on Tutsi-dominated rebels in east Zaire for access to Rwandan refugees with contacts between their leader and President Bill Clinton's envoy, aid officials said on Thursday.

They said Richard Bogosian, Clinton's special envoy to Africa's troubled Great Lakes region, contacted rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Wednesday by telephone and requested his support for the relief operation.
The aid officials also reported ongoing contacts in the region between U.S. diplomats and Kabila's aides.

The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR is awaiting Kabila's permission to use the airport in the rebel-held east Zairean town of Kisangani to start repatriating up to 20,000 refugees by plane and up to 80,000 others south of the city by truck.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns called on the rebels in Washington on Wednesday to cooperate with the UNHCR.

"This is a very serious situation," he said. "There have been good promises from Mr. Kabila and his forces, but they have not come through with the action necessary to give the U.N. access to the refugees, and some of those refugees have perished."
UNHCR says nearly 400 refugees have died of hunger, disease and exhaustion at a site south of Kisangani since March 16.

The Rwandan Hutus, among them former soldiers and extremist militiamen, fled to Zaire after 1994's Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis, setting the stage for much of today's conflict in Zaire, a mineral-rich former Belgian colony.

Zaire alleges that the rebels are aided by English-speaking Uganda and its Tutsi allies in Rwanda, which has developed close ties with Washington after the ouster of the genocidal Hutu government, a former political and military ally of France.
The latest U.S. diplomacy comes ahead of talks expected in South Africa between the rebels and representatives of Zaire's ailing ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, whom they have vowed to topple.
Washington supported Mobutu, 66, during the Cold War era but has kept him at arm's length since the mid-1980s.

In a government line-up unveiled on Thursday, Zaire's new prime minister, opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, earmarked six ministries for the rebels -- foreign affairs, defence, budget, planning, foreign trade and agriculture.
Mobutu, stricken with prostate cancer, has seen his grip on the sprawling Central African nation weakened by advances by the rebels, who took up arms in October.
He has kept his opponents guessing on what he intends to do with his remaining power. He named Tshisekedi, a veteran opponent, on Wednesday. He had sacked him from the post in 1993.
Said one diplomat: "This is Zaire, a continually churning pot. But it's not over. It's going to be a rollercoaster for at least another year."
"If you sit down and play poker with Mobutu, you'd better count your fingers when you leave the table."
